claims.text: Dependabot's PRs, all on a weekly interval, cover NuGet, pub (Dart), GitHub Actions and Docker base images; the docker ecosystem lists only /DonHang.Api, /DonHang.Notifications, /DonHang.Payments, /fake-gateway and /lab, not images named in docker-compose.yml such as Keycloak's.

Every component a team runs itself brings recurring work: upgrades and security fixes, backups and restore tests, monitoring, capacity (acting on it, e.g. limiting data retention), and someone who knows it when it fails; it repeats whether or not anything breaks.
claims.source_hint: Outline item 1; docs/team/self-run-components.md @ stage-3 lines 3-5, line 15 (Prometheus retention)

claims.text: Recurring work with no named owner tends not to get done at all: nobody watches for the release, so nobody starts the upgrade; each component needs a person who follows its releases and is called when it fails.

A managed service is software a provider runs for you, such as a managed database or a hosted message broker; it trades recurring work for a fee, less control (usually including when maintenance happens) and data on the provider's machines.
claims.source_hint: Outline item 4; glossary managed-service; docs/team/self-run-components.md @ stage-3 lines 6-8; k8s.l2.database-in-the-cluster summary line 3

claims.text: A managed service does not take all operating work: the team still chooses settings, watches how its own code uses the service, plans around provider-scheduled maintenance and version changes, and checks it can get its data back.
self-run-components.md table (lines 10-16): columns component, why self-run, recurring work, owner, managed option; rows PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, Keycloak, Prometheus/Grafana/Loki, Mailpit.

PostgreSQL row: patch upgrade each quarter, daily backup, WAL archived continuously, monthly restore test, watch disk space and connections; owner backend developers in turns; managed option: provider handles backups, copies and upgrades.

Keycloak row: frequent upgrades and security fixes because it is the entrance to the system; back up its realm (sign-in settings) and database; rotate signing keys; owner the team lead; managed option the paid sign-in service, option C of ADR 0009.

Mailpit catches every email in the lab and sends none; nobody owns it; sending email to customers is a capability still to buy, after an evaluation like payment-gateway-evaluation.md, before real customers.

In Compose Keycloak starts with start-dev (line 435) and KC_DB/KC_DB_URL point it at the keycloak database on db (lines 442-445), so its data and signing keys survive a new container and are backed up with the other databases.

Keycloak's start-dev runs it in development mode, meant for trying it out, not production; --import-realm imports realms (Keycloak's unit of sign-in settings) from files in its import directory at start.
claims.source_hint: Keycloak Server guide 'Configuring Keycloak' (start-dev vs start); 'Importing and exporting realms' (--import-realm at startup)

claims.text: In the staging cluster no database is configured for Keycloak (start-dev, no KC_DB), so it keeps its data inside its container and loses it when the Pod is replaced.

claims.text: Running Keycloak for real needs a production start with hostname and TLS configured, a database of its own with backups, and someone following its patches.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/self-run-components.md @ stage-3 lines 20-22; Keycloak guide 'Configuring Keycloak for production' (hostname, TLS required by start)

Much recurring work does not grow in step with the system (same release-note reading and test run at any size), while a fee growing with users (ADR 0009's paid sign-in) is smallest when small. Self-running is cheaper when the team knows the component and has time, or no managed option fits.
claims.source_hint: Outline misconception 3; docs/adr/0009 @ stage-3 (fee grows with number of users)
